en: May Sarasvatī, who is entirely white and who is like a female swan in the forest of the lotus-faces of the four-faced one, sport for a long time in my mind.
Having condensed the earlier treatises and observed actual literary practices, we compose this definition of poetry according to our own ability.
In this world, the course of worldly affairs proceeds entirely through the grace of speech alone—both that of those who have been instructed by the learned and that of the learned themselves.
This entire triple world would be born into blinding darkness, were it not for the light called "Word" (Śabda), which shines throughout the duration of saṃsāra.
Behold: having obtained the mirror of literature—the reflection of the glory of the first kings—this [glory] does not perish of its own accord, even in their absence.
It is recorded by the wise that speech, when properly employed, is like a cow that milks all desires; yet, when improperly employed, that very same speech proclaims the ox-like nature of its speaker.
Therefore, not even the slightest defect in poetry should ever be overlooked; for even a beautiful body may become repulsive because of a single leprous spot.
How can a person who is ignorant of the treatises distinguish between virtues and faults? Does a blind man have the capacity to perceive the differences in forms?
Therefore, with the aim of instructing living beings, the wise have composed the rules for the composition of speech through its various paths.
By them, both the body and the ornaments of poems have been demonstrated. First, the body is a sequence of words delimited by a desired meaning.
It is established as being of exactly three kinds: verse (padya), prose (gadya), and mixed (miśra). Verse consists of four lines, and it is of two types: metrical (vṛtta) and prosodic (jāti).
The entire treatise on prosody has been demonstrated therein; that science is a boat for those wishing to enter the deep ocean of poetry.
1 [The Root Text of the Kāvyādarśa] The *muktaka*, *kulaka*, *kośa*, and *saṃghāta*—such are the varieties of verse not mentioned here, as they are merely portions of the *sargabandha*.
A composition consisting of cantos is called a mahākāvya; its definition is as follows: its opening consists of a benediction, a salutation, or a statement of the subject matter.

Whether derived from historical narratives or otherwise, it must always have a virtuous basis, be directed toward the fruit of the four aims of human life, and feature a hero who is both clever and noble.
By means of descriptions of cities, oceans, mountains, seasons, and the rising of the moon and sun; and by means of garden parties, water-sports, drinking bouts, and the festivals of love.
[The plot is developed] through separations and marriages, descriptions of the birth of a prince, as well as by means of counsel, envoys, expeditions, sacrifices, and the triumph of the hero.
It is adorned, not condensed, continuous with rasa and bhāva, composed of cantos that are not overly long, written in melodious meters, and well-joined in their transitions.
Poetry that is endowed with diverse narratives throughout and possesses fine ornaments arises as a delight for the world, enduring even beyond the end of a kalpa.

A poem is not rendered defective by the absence of some of its constituent parts here, provided that there is perfection in those elements that have been employed, which satisfies those who know the art.
Having first introduced the hero according to his virtues, the subsequent repudiation of his enemies—this is the path that is naturally beautiful.
Even when describing the lineage, valor, learning, and other qualities of an enemy, our hearts are delighted by the narration of the hero’s excellence resulting from his victory over that foe.

A continuous sequence of words without metrical feet is prose (*gadya*), which consists of two varieties: the *ākhyāyikā* and the *kathā*. Of these two, it is said that the *ākhyāyikā*— [The remainder of the verse follows: "Is [a work] where the author reveals his own name, and where the narrative is told by himself or by another. || 1.25 || In this regard, some say that the *ākhyāyikā* is a story where the author reveals his own name, while others say it is where the narrative is told by the author himself or by another. However, there is no difference between the two regarding the nature of the subject matter; rather, the distinction lies in the manner of composition. Furthermore, some maintain that the *ākhyāyikā* is characterized by the inclusion of verses (*gāthā*) and the like, whereas the *kathā* is otherwise. But this is not so, for such features are found in both. Therefore, the distinction between the two is merely conventional. As for the *kathā*, its definition is as follows: "A *kathā* is a composition where the narrative is told by another, and where the author does not reveal his own name. || 1.26 || In this case, the term "another" refers to someone other than the author. It is called a *kathā* because it tells a story (*kathayati*). Since it is a specific type of *kathā*, it is termed a *kathā* (in the singular). This is because the word *kathā* is used here in the sense of a particular instance of the genre, just as one speaks of a "cow" (*go*) to refer to a specific animal. Alternatively, it may be understood as a collective singular, similar to the term *śruti*. Thus, the *kathā* is defined as a composition where the narrative is told by another and the author's name is not revealed. Examples of this are the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, the *Vetālapañcaviṃśatikā*, and the *Śukasaptati*. However, some say that the *kathā* is a story where the author does not reveal his own name, while the *ākhyāyikā* is where he does. Others say that the *kathā* is told by another, while the *ākhyāyikā* is told by the author himself or by another. Yet others claim that the *kathā* is characterized by the inclusion of verses and the like, while the *ākhyāyikā* is otherwise. But this is incorrect, as such characteristics are present in both. Therefore, the distinction between the two is purely conventional. As for the *kathā*: "A *kathā* is a composition where the narrative is told by another, and where the author does not reveal his own name. || 1.26 || In this context, "another" means someone other than the author. It is called a *kathā* because it narrates a story. Since it is a specific variety of *kathā*, it is designated as a *kathā* (singular), just as the word *go* is used to denote a specific cow. Or, it may be taken as a collective singular, like the term *śruti*. Thus, the *kathā* is defined as a work where the narrative is told by another and the author remains anonymous. Examples include the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, the *Vetālapañcaviṃśatikā*, and the *Śukasaptati*. However, some assert that the *kathā* is where the author does not reveal his name, and the *ākhyāyikā* is where he does. Others hold that the *kathā* is told by another, while the *ākhyāyikā* is told by the author himself or by another. Still others claim that the *kathā* includes verses and so forth, whereas the *ākhyāyikā* does not. But this is not right, for such features exist in both. Consequently, the distinction between them is merely a matter of convention. As for the *kathā*: "A *kathā* is a composition where the narrative is told by another, and where the author does not reveal his own name. || 1.26 || Here, "another" refers to anyone other than the author. Whether these [praises] are spoken by the hero himself or by another, there is no fault here in the manifestation of one's own qualities, for this proclaims a reality that has actually occurred.
Moreover, no fixed rule is observed there either, because it is uttered by others as well; whether another person speaks or oneself, what could possibly be the cause of distinction?

The presence of the *vaktra* and *aparavaktra* meters, as well as the inclusion of breath-like pauses (*socchvāsatva*), serves as the distinguishing mark of an *ākhyāyikā*; however, these features may also occur incidentally within *kathās*.

Why is there no entry [of a pause] at the beginning of the *vaktra* and *apavaktra* verses as there is for the *āryā* and other meters? Furthermore, even if a distinction were clearly perceived, what would it matter if there were a *lambha* or an *ucchvāsa*?
The First Chapter. Thus, the two designations "Kathā" and "Ākhyāyikā" constitute a single genre marked by two names; all other remaining types of narrative will be included within this very category.

The abduction of a maiden, battle, separation, and the rise [of prosperity], and so forth, are exactly like those found in epic compositions (*sargabandha*); these are not indeed distinctive qualities [of the campū].

A mark produced by a poet’s creative imagination does not become faulty even when applied elsewhere; for what indeed cannot serve as a gateway for those of perfected self toward the attainment of their desired goals?
The mixed forms include the *nāṭaka* and others, which are explained in detail elsewhere; there also exists a certain type known as *campū*, consisting of both prose and verse.
Furthermore, authoritative scholars declare that this entire realm of speech is fourfold: Sanskrit, Prākṛta, Apabhraṃśa, and Mixed.

That which is called *saṃskṛta* is the divine speech described by the great seers (*maharṣi*s). From it arises the *tadbhava*, that which is similar to it (*tatsama*), and the regional (*deśī*)—thus manifold is the system of *prākṛta*.
They know the language based on Mahārāṣṭra as the most excellent Prākṛta; it is the ocean of jewels of well-spoken verses, wherein the Setubandha and other works are composed.
Śaurasenī, Gauḍī, Lāṭī, and others of that kind, are designated as "Prākṛta" in common usage.
The speech of Ābhīras and others is known as *apabhraṃśa* in poetic works; however, in the technical treatises (*śāstra*), everything other than *saṃskṛta* is designated as *apabhraṃśa*.

Sanskrit consists of works such as the *sargabandha* (epic poems); Prākṛt consists of works such as the *skandhaka*; Apabhraṃśa consists of works such as the *osara*; and the mixed style consists of works such as the *nāṭaka*.
For the *Bṛhatkathā* is composed in all languages as well as in Sanskrit; those seeking marvelous meaning call it the *Bhūtabhāṣāmayī*.
Lāsya, cchalita, śampā, and so forth are for the purpose of being seen, while others are merely for being heard; thus, this twofold path has been described.
There are many paths of speech with subtle differences from one another; among them, the Vaidarbha and Gauḍīya styles are described as having clearly distinct characteristics.
Cohesion, clarity, evenness, sweetness, delicacy, explicitness of meaning, loftiness, vigor, splendor, and composure.
Thus, the ten qualities are considered the life-breaths of the Vaidarbha style; their opposite is generally observed in the Gauḍa path.

[1.42] The *śliṣṭa* (closely knit) style is that which is not touched by looseness and consists primarily of syllables with few breath-forces (*alpaprāṇa*), as in the example: "A garland of *mālatī* flowers, thick with swarms of restless bees."

The Gauḍas, through their perception of alliteration (*anuprāsa*), have prescribed that [the *mālatī* flower] because of its heavy composition; whereas the Vaidarbhas say, "A cluster of *mālatī* flowers has been trampled by bees."
"The mark of the moon, like a blue lotus, being endowed with clarity, spreads its splendor"—such is a statement that is pleasing because it accords with what is well-known.

The Gauḍīyas maintain that even a word that is not deeply conventionalized is considered "vyutpanna" (learned/derivative), as in the example: "the white-rayed moon, whose mark resembles a lotus that is not excessively pale."
Your compositions are uniform and free from unevenness; they consist of soft, clear, and middling styles, arising from the arrangement of syllables that are soft, clear, or mixed.
The Malaya breeze approaches me, rendered eloquent by the warbling of cuckoos and sprinkled with clear droplets from the water of leaping, spray-throwing cascades.
The gentle Malaya breeze, fragrant with the scent of sandalwood and intimate with it, vies with the breath from the faces of beautiful women who have obstructed my fortitude.
Thus, disregarding this inequality and regarding the profusion of poetic figures and ornaments as paramount, the eastern tradition of poetry flourished.
Sweetness resides not only in speech but also in the subject matter itself; by means of this, the wise are intoxicated, just as bees are by honey.

Whatever commonality is experienced through any particular sound, that indeed is *padāsatti* (proximity of words); when it possesses alliteration (*anuprāsa*), it brings forth aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Ever since this king, who is dear to the Brahmins, attained royal fortune, there has been a festival of Dharma in this world.
Thus, this [type of alliteration] is not favored by the Gauḍas, for they prefer alliteration; however, even more than alliteration, this is generally desired by the Vaidarbhas.

Alliteration (anuprāsa) is the repetition of phonemes both within quarters (pādas) and within words (padas), provided that it is not too remote [from the preceding sound] and serves to awaken the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of prior experience.
Upon the moon—the crest-ornament of the autumn night and possessing the splendor of a cluster of kunda flowers—the dark spot bears the beauty of a bee, resembling a sapphire.
O timid one, behold this beautiful lunar orb in the sky; it is like my own heart, which, overcome by love, is mercilessly intent on slaying me.

First Chapter: Thus they desire alliteration (*anuprāsa*) when the sounds are heard at intervals that are not too far apart; but [they do not accept it] in a case such as "The moon is like the lotus-face of Rāmā."
Love has become harsh; the beloved is wicked; our bodies and anger have grown thin; pride has vanished; passion has increased; delusion has arisen; and the vital breaths have departed.
Such harshness of construction and looseness as these he restrains; therefore, the Southerners do not employ alliteration in this manner.
The wise know that *yamaka* (rhyme) consists precisely of the repetition [of syllables] within the scope of word-groups; however, because it is not invariably sweet, it will be explained later.
Granted that every ornament sprinkles flavor upon the meaning; nevertheless, it is non-vulgarity alone that bears the greater weight of this burden.
"O maiden, why do you not desire me who desires you?"—such vulgar speech, centered on worldly objects, leads only to a loss of aesthetic flavor.

"O fair-eyed one, it is true that the outcaste Kandarpa is merciless toward me; yet by good fortune, he is free from envy toward you"—this meaning, being non-vulgar, brings forth aesthetic flavor (rasa).

Even in the case of sound, vulgarity certainly exists when there is the mention of what is unfit for refined society; as, for example, a word beginning with the letter *ya* when describing the celebration of sexual passion.
Furthermore, that which causes misunderstanding—either through the function of word-connection or through the meaning of the sentence—is *grāmya* (vulgar), as in: "She who is dear to you."
"A man who has struck a hard blow is one of great prowess"—such sayings as these they do not praise in either of the two paths.

The use of terms such as *bhaginī* (sister) and *bhagavatī* (venerable lady) is approved in all cases; this distinctness is called sweetness (*mādhurya*), which is the quality of delicacy (*sukumāratā*).

In this [context], that which consists mostly of non-harsh syllables is desired as "delicate" (sukumāra); furthermore, the fault of looseness in composition (bandha-śaithilya) has been shown to exist in all [styles].
Forming circles with their tails and singing sweet songs with their throats, the peacocks dance at this time when the sky is garlanded with clouds.
Thus, the meaning itself is not forceful, nor is the ornament of that sort; yet, by its very delicacy, this [poem] ascends to the mouths of the wise.

"It is radiant," so others adorned it; even that which was difficult to undertake was bound [together]. "In an instant, the faction of the kṣatriyas has been utterly destroyed"—thus [it was proclaimed].

The source for this is Kāvyādarśa 1.64: "Clarity of meaning consists in the fact that the meaning is not subject to other interpretations, as in the verse: 'The earth was lifted from the ocean, which had become red with the blood of serpents trampled by his hooves.'"
"The earth was lifted from the ocean by the Great Boar"—when only this much is stated, the fact that it was the blood of a serpent [the demon Hiraṇyākṣa] remains to be inferred.
People do not hold such [a view] in high regard in either of the two paths; for a cognition that transgresses the principles of words is not auspicious.
When some quality characterized by excellence is perceived in what has been expressed, that is called the "Noble" (udāra); by this, the path of poetry is graced.
O Lord, the piteous gaze of supplicants that has fallen upon Your face even once never again looks toward the face of another in such a state.
Thus, in this statement regarding renunciation, its excellence is clearly perceived; by this very same path, other matters governed by similar principles should be inferred.
Some maintain that the *udāra* (magnificent) style is characterized by praiseworthy epithets; for example, "the playful lotus," "the sporting lake," and "the golden armlet."
Abundance of compounds is the very lifeblood of prose; even in verse, this alone is the ultimate resort for those who are not from the South.
Through the combination of many or few, and heavy or light [syllables], the noble *dṛśya* (visual spectacle) takes on various high and low forms in works such as the *ākhyāyikā*.

With the entire expanse of the sun’s rays cast down upon the summit of the setting mountain, the western quarter appeared like a woman wearing a beautiful, copper-red garment draped over her full breasts.
Thus, even in verse, the Easterners compose powerful expressions; others, however, desire a power of speech that is unconfused and heart-pleasing, as follows:
Whose mind, already afflicted by passion, will the wine not further disturb—wine that clings like the glow of twilight to the slopes of her breasts?
It is "beloved" (kānta), because it is beloved by the entire world, as it does not transcend worldly matters; and this is seen both in the narration of news and in poetic descriptions.
Those alone are truly called "homes" which a mass of asceticism such as yours honors with the purifying dust of your feet.
O lady of faultless limbs, as these two breasts of yours expand, there is no sufficient space within the interval of your creeper-like arms.

When a certain meaning is intended to be expressed by superimposing upon it an extreme transcendence of the world, as it were, the wise are exceedingly delighted by it, whereas others are not, just as [the wise are moved by a particular beauty].
From this day forward, our home shall be worthy of worship like the abode of a god, its every impurity washed away by the falling dust of your feet.
The Creator, without even considering that the space he had fashioned was so small, has ordained that your breasts shall expand in this manner.
This has been called "exaggerated speech" (atyukti); this is the method cherished by the Gauḍas, whereas that previously set forth belongs to the essence of another path.
When one property is correctly applied to another, in accordance with worldly convention, that is known as *samādhi*, as for example: [the application of "blue" to a lotus].
"The night-lotuses close and the day-lotuses open"—thus, through the superimposition of the activity of eyes, the word [for "lotus"] is employed as its designator.
Expressions such as "spitting," "sighing," or "vomiting," when based on figurative usage (gauṇavṛtti), are exceedingly beautiful; otherwise, they sink into the level of vulgarity.
Having drunk sparks of fire shaken from the mouths of the horses, the lotuses seem to vomit them back again through their mouths, which have disgorged crimson pollen.
Thus, "the bride spits out what is pleasant as well as what is unpleasant"—this is considered an instance of simultaneous superimposition (adhyāsa) of multiple attributes.
Exhausted by the heavy burden of their wombs, these rows of clouds, thundering aloud, rest upon the lap of the mountain plateau.
Sleeping on a lap, sighing, heaviness, and exhaustion—these many symptoms of pregnancy are shown here in another [context].
This very quality called *samādhi* is the essence of poetry; even the entire community of poets lives by depending upon this one alone.
Thus, these two paths are distinct based on the definition of their essential natures; however, their specific subdivisions, which exist for every poet, cannot be fully described.
There is a vast difference between the sweetness of milk, molasses, and so forth; nevertheless, even Sarasvatī herself would not be able to describe it.
Innate genius, extensive and stainless learning, and unremitting application—these are the causes of excellence in poetry.
Even if there exists no marvelous intuition that follows from the continuity of past impressions (*vāsanā*), speech cultivated through learning and effort certainly bestows some kind of grace.

Therefore, those who desire fame must indeed worship Sarasvatī incessantly and without sloth in due order; for even when their poetic talent is meager, people who have exerted effort are able to move within the assemblies of the learned.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Classification of Styles," in the *Kāvyādarśa* composed by Ācārya Daṇḍin. In the second chapter of the *Kāvyādarśa*, those qualities that enhance the beauty of poetry are called "ornaments" (*alaṃkāra*). Although these have been conceptualized even until now, he will describe them in their entirety as they truly are.
However, the seed of these conceptual constructions was already demonstrated by previous teachers; this effort of ours is merely to refine that very [seed].
Some figures of speech have already been mentioned for the purpose of distinguishing the paths; now, another collection of common figures of speech is being demonstrated.

Description of intrinsic nature (svabhāvākhyāna), simile (upamā), metaphor (rūpaka), the lamp-ornament (dīpaka) and its repetition (āvṛtti), the parable (ākṣepa), corroboration by another matter (arthāntaranyāsa), contrast (vyatireka), and the description of the extraordinary (vibhāvanā). ||4||

Conciseness (samāsa), hyperbole (atiśaya), poetic fancy (utprekṣā), cause (hetu), the subtle (sūkṣma), the drop (lava), sequence (krama), the lovable (preyaḥ), the sentiment-filled (rasavat), the forceful (ūrjasvin), the periphrasis (paryāyokta), and the composed (samāhita).
Hyperbole, concealment, the figure based on a double-entendre, Equal Pairing, Contradiction, Indirect Praise, Dispraise through Praise, and Illustration; |||

The second chapter: Joint Description (sahokti), Exchange (parivṛtti), Benediction (āśīḥ), the Interwoven (saṃkīrṇa), and then the Vivid (bhāvika). Thus have the ornaments of speech been demonstrated by the ancient masters.

The figure of speech known as *svabhāvokti* (description of inherent nature) and *jāti* (universal description), which directly reveal the various states of the forms of objects, is an ornament (*alaṃkāra*), as for example: [Example: "The young elephant, with its trunk raised high, its ears flapping, its tail twitching, and its eyes rolling, enters the lotus pond, trumpeting loudly. In this verse, the natural characteristics and activities of the young elephant are described in detail, constituting the figures of *svabhāvokti* and *jāti*. Thus, these are considered poetic ornaments.
With beaks that are copper-red and curved, wings that are tenderly green, and throats marked with three-colored stripes—these parrots possess sweet voices.
With a throat filled with cooing and rolling eyes, the pigeon, desiring to sport, embraces and kisses his beloved.
Causing horripilation on his limbs, producing bliss in his mind, and causing his eyes to close, this touch of the beloved proceeds.
With blackness upon his throat, holding a skull in his hand, and crowned by the moon, the bull-bannered Lord appeared with matted locks of glossy, coppery hue.
Such is the description of genus, action, quality, substance, and intrinsic nature; this alone holds sovereign sway in the technical treatises, and it is likewise desired in poetry.
Wherever a semblance of similarity is perceived in any manner whatsoever, that is called *upamā* (simile); its various elaborations are now demonstrated.
"O charming one, your palm is like a lotus that has not yet opened"—this is a direct simile based on dharma (quality), because it demonstrates a common quality directly.
"Your face is like a lotus, and your eyes are like blue water-lilies; this is indeed a *vastūpamā* (object-simile), characterized by a single common attribute that is explicitly stated."
"Because of your gift, the lotus has become as if blooming"—this is considered a "reversal simile" (*viparyāsopamā*) due to the inversion of common renown.
"Your face is like a lotus, and a lotus is like your face"—this is the *anyonyopamā* (mutual simile), which proclaims the mutual excellence of the two.
"Your face is equal only to the lotus, and not to anything else"—this is *niyamopamā* (restricted simile), because it excludes comparison with other things.
"The lotus follows after your face; as for any other such thing, let it exist if it does—let it be its maker. This is "unrestricted simile" (aniyamopamā).

There is also the simile of conjunction (*samuccayopamā*), such as this: "Your face does not equal the moon by its beauty alone; it also conforms to the moon through the action known as 'gladdening'."

2 [Root Text of the Kāvyādarśa] Root Text of the Kāvyādarśa: "Your face is seen only in you; the moon is seen in the sky. The difference is only this much and no other"—this is *atiśayopamā* (hyperbolic simile).
"The glory of her beauty resides in me alone"—enough with such boasts by the moon! Since that [beauty] exists in the lotus as well, this is a "Poetic Fancy Simile" (utprekṣitopamā).
"If there were some lotus with eyes as beautiful as yours, let it bear the splendor of your face"—this is the "marvelous simile" (*adbhutopamā*).
"O slender-limbed one, having imagined your face to be the moon, I run after even the moon out of longing for your face"—this is considered a simile of delusion (mohopamā).
"Is it a lotus with bees wandering within, or is it your face with its tremulous eyes? My mind wavers"—this is a simile based on doubt (*saṃśayopamā*).
The luster of the moon, which is surpassed by the lotus, does not produce the beauty of the moon; therefore, "this is indeed your face"—this is a simile of determination (nirṇayopamā).
"Your face is like a lotus—rivaling the cool-rayed moon, glorious, and fragrant"—this is known as a simile based on paronomasia (śleṣopamā).

That is "Equal Simile" (samānopamā) because it is expressed by words that possess the same form (*sarūpa*), as for example: "This cloud-bank in the garden is like a young girl, beautified by groves of *sāla* trees."
"The lotus has much pollen, and the moon is subject to waning; though your face is equal to these two, it is superior"—this is known as the "censuring simile" (nindopamā).
"The lotus of Brahmā and the moon borne upon the head of Śambhu—those two are equal to your face"; this is called praise-comparison (praśaṃsopamā).
"My mind desires to declare that your face is equal to the moon; let it be a merit or a defect—this they know as the *ācikhyāsopamā* (simile of the desire to declare)."
"The hundred-petaled lotus," "the autumnal moon," and "your face"—these three are mutually opposed; this is considered the simile of contradiction (virodhopamā).
"The power of the moon, being stained and dull, can never easily roar back in response"—this is indeed a simile of negation (*pratiṣedhopamā*).
"Your face is marked by deer-like eyes, and the moon is marked by a deer; nevertheless, the moon is merely equal [to your face] and does not surpass it"—this is a flattering simile (caṭūpamā).
"This is not a lotus; these two are not bees, but rather eyes"—because the similarity is so clearly evident, this is indeed a *tattvākhyānopamā* (a simile consisting of a statement of reality).
"Having transcended the ranks of both the moon and the lotus, your face became equal to itself alone"—this is the *asādhāraṇopamā* (the incomparable simile).
The second chapter: "Your face shines as if the essence of the radiance of all lotuses were gathered in one place"—this they know as the *abhūtopamā* (the impossible simile).
"Poison from the orb of the moon, fire from sandalwood, or harsh speech from this mouth"—such is an impossible simile (*asaṃbhāvitopamā*).
"Your touch is cool like sandalwood water, moonbeams, moonstones, and so forth"—this is a "many similes" (bahūpamā) figure, proclaiming your extraordinary excellence.
"O slender-limbed one, your face is as if carved out from the orb of the moon or extracted from the heart of a lotus"—this is *vikriyopamā* (metaphor of transformation).
"Vikrama bestowed splendor upon you, as the sun's heat does upon the day, as Pūṣan does upon the sky, and as the day does upon the sky"—this is the sequence of a string of similes (mālopamā).

If some sentence-meaning is compared with another sentence-meaning, that is *vākyārthopamā* (sentence-meaning simile); it is of two kinds, according as the word "like" (*iva*) occurs once or more than once.
Your face, with its steady eyes and the radiance of manifest teeth, shines like a lotus with visible filaments that appear to be trembling as they swirl.
Like a bee drinking repeatedly from a lotus, I took delight in drinking in the face of that slender-limbed woman, which was like a lotus to her lily-like form.

Having introduced some object, the presentation of another object possessing similar properties, such that a perception of similarity exists, is the *prativastūpamā* (simile by parallelism), as for example: The lotus is born from the mud; the moon is born from the ocean. Yet both are the cause of joy for the eyes of the world. In this verse, having first introduced the lotus and the moon as two distinct objects, the poet presents their common property—being the source of joy for the eyes of the world—thereby establishing a perception of similarity between them. This constitutes the figure of speech known as *prativastūpamā*.
Not even one like you has appeared among the kings born until now; indeed, there is no second tree of the *pārijāta*.
When one equalizes the inferior with the superior by means of a single action, that which they describe is known as *tulyayogopamā* (simile of equal conjunction), as for example: [text follows].
The enemy of Puloma keeps watch over heaven for its protection, while you do so for the earth; by him the Asuras are slain, and by you, arrogant kings.
"O King, you emulate the moon in beauty, the sun in splendor, and the ocean in fortitude"—this is considered a simile based on a cause (*hetūpamā*).
Neither a difference in gender or number, nor even inferiority or superiority, is sufficient to constitute a fault in a simile, provided that it causes no distress to the wise.
"This eunuch walks like a woman," "This woman speaks like a man," "He is as dear to me as my own life," or "Knowledge is like wealth acquired."
O protector of the earth, like you, the king of the gods shines resplendent;
by his splendor, this monarch is fully capable of ascending to the rank of the sun.
Such good fortune as this never indeed deserts him at any time; yet there is also a certain agitation in the performance, as is experienced by those skilled in speech.
The moon is white like a female swan; the sky is stainless like lakes; a soldier devoted to his master is like a dog; and a firefly shines like the sun.
Such things are avoided by the virtuous; let the cause for this be reflected upon by the wise themselves for the sake of discerning merits and faults.
The words *iva*, *vat*, *yathā*, *śabda*, as well as *samāna*, *nibha*, and *saṃnibha*; *tulya*, *saṃkāśa*, *nīkāśa*, *prakāśa*, *pratirūpaka*;
*pratipakṣa*, *pratidvandvin*, *pratyanīka*, and *virodhin*; and *sadṛk*, *sadṛśa*, *saṃvādin*, *sajātīya*, and *anuvādin* [all signify similarity].
Reflection, counterpart, similar, equal, and commensurate; possessing characteristics, resembling, appearing like, like, comparable, and illustrated by comparison.

Words such as *kalpadeśīya* and *deśya*, as well as those that are well-known synonyms or substitutes, and words that denote an equivalent or similar quality (*savarṇa*), or are equal in value (*tulita*), or express a meaning that is not inferior (*anyūnārthavādin*) [are also used].
And the compound *bahuvrīhi* occurs in such expressions as "moon-faced" (*śaśāṅkavadanā*) and the like, when one [the face] rivals, conquers, hates, harms, or roars back against [the moon].
He reviles, despises, torments, censures, mocks, strikes, laughs at, and envies.
It steals away his good fortune, it robs him of his splendor; it contends with him, and it even rivals him in the balance.
It places its foot upon his path, it enters his courtyard, it follows him, it clings to him, it imitates his character, and it opposes him.
And because it imitates that [object], words indicating similarity are called "similes" (upamā) by poets; they grant ease to the intellect.

Metaphor (rūpaka) is said to be a simile in which the distinction [between the object and the attribute] has become concealed; for example: "the vine-like arm, the lotus-like hand, the sprout-like foot."
The fingers were her young shoots, and the radiance of her nails was her flowers. Second Chapter: O Goddess of Spring, you are our visible presence, with your arms as your creepers.
This is called the "compound" (samasta) complete metaphor; "the smile is the moonlight of the moon-like face" is a metaphor that is both compound and partial (samastavyasta).
The kings bear upon their heads your lotus-feet, which possess rows of copper-colored petal-like fingers and filaments of light from the nails.

Having superimposed the nature of petals and so forth upon the fingers and so on, and the state of being a lotus upon the foot, by placing them in their appropriate positions, this is the *sakalarūpaka* (complete metaphor).
O passionate one, for no apparent reason, your face—with its sprout-like lower lip quivering—bears clusters of drops of perspiration that possess the luster of pearls.
Having turned the sweat into a cluster of blossoms and the lower lip into a sprout, her face here was not otherwise altered; thus, this is an "ornament of parts" (avayavarūpaka).
This lotus-face, with its trembling form, trickling perspiration, and blood-red eyes, reveals the state of intoxication.
Without transforming the other facial features, the face itself was turned into a lotus; therefore, this is an *avayavirūpaka* (part-whole metaphor).
By your face, with cheeks rosy from intoxication and eyes like red lotuses, even this deluded person has been made full of passion.
This is a *rūpaka* consisting of a single limb; likewise, two or more limbs may also be so represented here, where their combination or non-combination creates the distinction.
"This pleasure is radiant with the flowers of smiles and has the bees of flickering eyes"—thus, through the union of flowers and bees, a fitting metaphor is formed.

"This face has the moonlight of a tender smile and the blue lotuses of affectionate eyes"—this is called an "improper" (ayukta) metaphor (*rūpaka*), due to the incongruity between the moonlight and the lotuses.
When the transformation of the whole results from the transformation or non-transformation of its parts, a charming figure of speech called "Uneven Metaphor" (viṣamarūpaka) arises, as follows:
With its face like the moon, flushed with wine, and with its creeper-like eyebrows dancing, Love is fully capable of crushing the three worlds with you as his instrument.

Victorious is the foot of Hari, whose silken garment is the water of the daughter of Jahnu clinging to its crest, and which serves as the banner for the festival of joy of the gods who are now free from fear of the asuras.
If the form of a banner, complete with its specific attributes, is such as this, then by the application of that [form] to a foot [of a verse], this is "Metaphor with Attributes" (saviśeṣaṇarūpaka).

It does not close the lotuses, nor does it plunge into the sky. In this passage from the *Kāvyādarśa*, since the clouds and the elephants are not distinguished by their attributes (*dharma*), their connection is established solely through the action of "wandering" (*bhramaṇa*); thus, this is an instance of *śliṣṭārtha-dīpaka* (illuminator of double-meaning objects).
In this very manner, the wise should apply the same analysis to the remaining varieties of the *dīpaka* ornament.
The repetition of meaning, the repetition of words, and the repetition of both are also accepted as three distinct ornaments in the very same place where the *dīpaka* occurs, as follows.
The kadamba trees are blooming, the kuṭaja and arjuna trees are bursting open, the kandalī plants are unfolding, and the kakubha trees are budding.
The line of clouds stirs the flocks of peacocks, and today the god whose banner is the sea-monster stirs the hearts of young men with longing.
Having conquered the entire world, you sport here with your harem; your enemies, having gone to heaven, sport with the celestial nymphs.

The statement of prohibition is *ākṣepa* (paralipsis), which is threefold with respect to the three periods of time; furthermore, it is infinite because the varieties of what is being paralledized are infinite.
"The bodiless one conquers the universe with five flowery arrows"—this is indeed improbable; yet, the powers of things are truly wondrous.

When the cognition of the practice of yoga for the conquest of the bodiless one (Kāma) has already begun here by the force of its cause, and that [cognition] is then sublated, that is the "sublation of what has occurred" (*vṛttākṣepa*). ||122||
"Why do you place a blue lotus on your ear, O sweet-voiced one? Do you consider your sidelong glance insufficient for this task?"
While she was still placing a blue lotus upon her ear, she was thus restrained by her lover with these flattering words: "This is an act that projects the present."
I tell you the truth, my beloved: you shall not see me again with eyes reddened by the lac transferred from the kisses of another.
This was an anticipation of what was to come; for she, being exceedingly high-spirited, restrained him by thinking that some offense might perhaps be committed by him in the future.
O slender-limbed one, the softness that has grown upon your limbs is surely false; for if they were truly soft, why do they cause me such pain so unexpectedly?
This is an instance of *dharmākṣepa* (the denial of a property), wherein the lover has denied the softness of the woman's limbs by means of an action that is contrary to it.
By what means does this discrimination arise that "she is beautiful" and "she is mine"?
This is the second section. For only a flickering radiance is perceived; its substratum is not seen at all.

This is an *ākṣepa* (paralipsis) of the subject (*dharmī*), wherein the subject named "Prabhā" is implied; for here, the speaker intends to describe her form, which is exceedingly wonderful due to its latent disposition (*anuśaya*).
Your eyes are reddened, your sprout-like lower lip quivers, and your brows are arched; yet even so, I have no fear of you, for I am not wicked.
This is the "rejection of the cause" (kāraṇākṣepa), wherein the primary cause of fear—namely, one's own transgression—is here denied by a clever lover.
That beloved season has arrived from afar—the onset of the clouds; the *nicula* trees have been seen in full bloom, and yet I am not dead—what indeed is this?
That is the "suggestion of an effect" (kāryākṣepa), because it averts the effect—death—by introducing its cause: the arrival of the terrible clouds.
Your journey will not cause me long-lasting distress; if you must go where you must go, enough of this apprehension on your part.
In this way, by means of a request for permission, the departure of the beloved is censured; since she thus indicates her own death, this is called "censure with permission" (sānujñākṣepa).
You shall obtain much wealth, and there will be happiness and safety on your path; nor is there any danger to my life. Nevertheless, my dear, do not go.
When she, by rejecting the reasons that would obstruct her beloved's journey, restrains him solely through her authority, that is such an "implied authority" (prabhutvākṣepa).
My hope for life is strong, while my hope for wealth is weak. Go or stay, my beloved; I have disclosed my own condition.
This is the *anādārākṣepa* (insinuation of disregard), wherein words expressive of disregard are employed by a woman who is actually attached, in order to obstruct the departure of her beloved.
Go, O beloved, if you must go; may your paths be auspicious. May my birth also take place in that very place where you have gone.
Thus, by means of a benediction, there is an implied rejection; for, while indicating her own condition, the beloved’s departure is forbidden.
If your journey is indeed true, let some other [means] be taken by you; for today I am hemmed in by Death, who watches for a vulnerable moment.
Thus, this is the "harsh rebuke" (paruṣākṣepa), because the departure of her beloved is rebuked by a woman overcome with love through the use of harsh words.
If you are to go, O Karṇa, depart quickly; for the cries of those who have uttered them from the mouths of their afflicted kinsmen—which obstruct one's departure—are already reaching you.

3 [Root Text of the Kāvyādarśa] This is indeed a form of "Suggestion by Assistance" (sācivyākṣepa), wherein that which is prohibited is performed as an act of assistance by one who is intensely impassioned at the departure of her beloved.
"Go," I wish to say, O my beloved, for I desire your welfare; yet the words "Do not go" issue from my mouth—what can I do?
That is the "futility of effort," because it demonstrates the pointlessness of an effort directed toward an undesired object, since it results in a contrary outcome.
Tell me of the departure of that love which grows angry even at the blinking of an eyelash as an obstacle to a moment’s sight; its departure is desired by me for his sake.
This is the "interjection of dependence on another" (paravaśākṣepa), wherein a journey is forbidden by her who is dependent on love, due to the addition of another purpose.
"I shall endure separation, O Lord; give me the ointment for invisibility, so that when my eyes are anointed with it, Kandarpa, the striker, will not see me."
Having proposed a difficult means of livelihood, he is then restrained; such is called "the objection based on a means" (*upāyākṣepa*), as in the phrase "the departure of the husband."
"O beloved, even though my voice has set out with the thought 'I am going,' it remains here with you now due to your dull affection; how can this be?"

This is an instance of *roṣākṣepa* (restraint through anger), wherein a departure initiated by a beloved is prevented by a woman whose self is constrained by overflowing affection and who is overcome with agitation.
The innocent girl fainted merely upon hearing her lover’s words of departure; having regained consciousness and seeing her beloved, she says: "Why have you returned so late?"
"Thus, the movement of the lover is interrupted by a fainting fit arising at that moment; such is the interruption by fainting (mūrchākṣepa) on the part of the timid-eyed woman."
Neither was it struck, nor placed upon the ear, nor offered as honey by women; rather, the blue lotus of your enemies withered away within their very long ponds.

This is an *ākṣepa* (preclusion) accompanied by compassion, as if toward a lotus endowed with compassion; for, by demonstrating a state of woe, it turns away from an action appropriate to that [lotus].
No wealth has been accumulated, no knowledge acquired, no austerity performed; and yet our entire life has passed away.

This is the implication of the latent tendencies (anuśaya), because it is shown here that for one whose life has ended, there is a cessation of the acquisition of wealth and so forth immediately following those latent tendencies.
Since this moon of your face exists— whose essence is nectar, which detests the lotuses, and whose pupils are tender— what need is there for another moon?
The second chapter: Thus, the primary moon is negated by demonstrating qualities residing in the secondary moon that are similar to them; such is the "negation through punning" (śliṣṭākṣepa).
Is this an autumnal cloud, or is it a flock of swans? That which is heard is resonant with the sound of anklets; therefore, it is not a rain-cloud.
Thus, this is the objection based on doubt; for the doubt is dispelled by that quality which is easily acquired by swans and untouched by the nature of clouds.
How wonderful that even though you have pervaded the entire universe, your prowess remains unsated! When indeed is satisfaction ever seen in a blazing fire?

This is the "suggestion of another matter" (*arthāntarākṣepa*) which was introduced [in the previous section] and is now being set aside, because here there is the observation of a matter of wonder that possesses a quality in common with it.
O Lord of Men, you are never praised with the words "you give," because supplicants take your wealth as if it were their own.
An objection such as this and others like it is known as the "objection based on a reason" (hetvākṣepa). In this same manner, other varieties [of objections] can also be inferred.
That should be known as *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by another matter), wherein, having introduced a certain subject, there is the presentation of another matter capable of establishing it.

Pervading all, yet abiding in particulars; joined by conjunction, yet possessing contradiction; acting improperly, yet having a disciplined self; both consistent and inconsistent—such is the reversal.
Such varieties as these have been characterized in the practical applications; this series of examples is presented in order to clarify their specific forms.
Behold, even the two blessed ones who are the eyes of the world, the sun and the moon, are going to their setting; by whom can destiny be transgressed?
These clouds remove the torment of embodied beings; indeed, the very attainment of self by the great is for the sake of allaying the suffering of others.
The Malaya breeze generates joy in the world; indeed, one endowed with courtesy becomes dear to everyone.
Even though he is stained, this maker of night brings delight to the world; for even though he possesses faults, the lord of the twice-born bestows grace upon others.
Even the sound of bees emerging from their throats due to the drinking of honey becomes harsh to the ears of lovers; such is the nature of sin.
This bed of lotus petals burns my limbs; indeed, is it not fitting that its very nature be a substitute for fire?
Let the moon wane at will; why does spring distress me? Indeed, it is improper for the fragrant breeze to perform such a foul deed.
Even the night-lotuses lead to burning; how much more so the bed of day-lotuses! For one who is under the grasp of the sun cannot be gentle even toward those dwelling in the mansions of the moon.
When a similarity between two things is either explicitly stated by words or understood through implication, the description of their difference therein is called *vyatireka* (distinction).
In qualities such as fortitude, beauty, and profundity, you are equal to the ocean; the only difference between you and him lies in your physical form.
Thus,
this is a single negative concomitance (vyatireka) based on a property residing in one [locus], because it brings about the cognition of a distinction that resides in both.
Both you and this ocean are deep and possess unbroken shores; yet he is like black collyrium, while you possess the luster of gold.
This is an instance of mutual exclusion (ubhayavyatireka), wherein the two qualities that serve as differentiators—blackness and tawny-brown—are shown here separately.
Both you and the ocean are difficult to restrain, both possess great strength and splendor; yet this is the extent of the difference between you two: he is inert by nature, while you are alert.

Since this very [figure] consists of a combination (śleṣa), let it be understood as *saṃśleṣa* (combination); both of those [types], namely with censure (*sākṣepa*) and with a reason (*sahetu*), are now demonstrated.
Though it is stable, steadfast, and a mine of jewels, the ocean,
being turbid, can never equal your excellence.
Even though he supports the entire earth with its mountains, islands, and oceans, Śeṣa is inferior to you because he serves as the bearer for those who are not serpents.

This [type of] vyatireka (contrast) involves a similarity based on the verbal expression; there is also that which possesses a similarity implied [rather than expressed], and that is what is being discussed here.
Between these two—your face and the lotus—there is indeed a distinction: the lotus grows in water, while your face rests upon you.
This pair of eyes of yours, O gazelle-eyed one, is devoid of the play of eyebrows and untouched by the flush of intoxication, yet it is adorned with those very qualities.

In the former [type], there is merely the statement of a distinction; in this one, an additional quality is shown. Furthermore, another variety is demonstrated, which consists of a contrast with a similar object.
Second Chapter: Your face and the lotus are both in full bloom and fragrant; yet the lotus is frequented by bees, while your face has tremulous eyes.
This moon is the crest-jewel of the sky; this swan is the ornament of the water; this sky is garlanded with stars; and this water is filled with blossoming lilies.

In this [verse], a distinction is made between the sky and water—which possess a perceived similarity through their manifest whiteness—and between the moon and the swan, both of which are recognized as pure.

In the preceding case, as with the word [“bee”], there is similarity in both instances; however, the distinguishing factor is that while [the bee] is common to both [the eyes and the face], the [actual] bees and eyes are distinct, whereas here there is a negation of anything similar to them.
Youth is a darkness born of the sky that obstructs the vision of young men; it cannot be dispelled by the light of jewels, yet it is not to be overcome even by the rays of the sun.

This is an exclusion based on genus: this darkness belongs to the class of darkness, being equal [to other instances] by virtue of obstructing vision, though it is distinguished from others as observed.
When, by the exclusion of a well-known cause, some other cause or even inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*) is imagined in a given instance, that is *vibhāvanā* (the figure of "peculiar causation").
The world was enchanting: its geese were neither drunk nor yellowed, the sky was stainless without being wiped clean, and the water was pure without being clarified.
O beautiful one, your gaze is neither anointed nor blackened; your brow is neither bent nor lowered; and this lower lip of yours is neither stained with rouge nor reddish.
Even if intoxication and the like were produced by drinking [liquor] and other causes, or were causeless, there is no contradiction here, because that is not what is intended to be expressed.
The face is naturally fragrant, and the body is beautiful without artifice; yet the moon is an enemy without cause, and the god of love is a foe without provocation.
In this instance, the cause is directly negated by words such as "by nature" (*nisarga*); yet, the result—such as fragrance—is stated. That is *vibhāvanā*.
Having intended some particular object, the mention of another object similar to it—because of its concise nature—is desired as *samāsokti* (speech by ellipsis).
Behold, like a bee drinking honey at will from a full-blown lotus, he kisses a bud whose fragrance has not yet unfolded.
Thus, in this case, the movement of desire is observed in a certain young girl toward a passionate man who has engaged in amorous play with a mature woman.

Even when the qualifiers are identical in form, they may differ merely in their substantive; there is this [type of simile], and there is also another where the qualifiers are both different and non-different. (Kāvyādarśa, Root Text)
With its roots firmly established, nourishing supplicants incessantly with its abundance of fruit, and providing dense shade—this very great tree has been reached by me.
By good fortune, I have found this tree, which possesses an abundance of branches, is rich in fruits and flowers, and is lofty and firm.
In both cases, a certain male is described as being a tree; all the properties are common to both, yet in the former case there is one [additional] property, while in the latter there are two.
Alas, this ocean, whose nature is sweet and from which the company of venomous serpents has departed, is being dried up by time.
Thus, this is a case of *pūrvasamāsokti* (synecdoche by the prior), because it indicates the destruction of a man equal to the ocean through the negation of his former attributes.
Thus concludes the cycle of *samāsokti* (synecdoche).
When the intention to express a particularity transcends the limits of the world, that is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), the highest of poetic ornaments, as for example:
Carrying garlands of jasmine, with sandalwood paste applied to all their limbs and wearing silk garments, the women going to meet their lovers are not visible in the moonlight.
The abundance of moonlight has been described as possessing excellence; now, something is illustrated in order to clarify such states as doubt and intensification.
O beloved, even today the doubt as to whether your waist exists or does not exist—situated between your breasts and your hips—does not cease.
O slender-waisted one, it can be determined that you possess a waist, solely because the presence of the weight of your breasts would otherwise be inexplicable.
Oh King, how vast is the interior of the three worlds! For even the mass of your glory, which is impossible to contain, finds room within it.
They say that among all other ornaments, this liberation called "Excellence" (atiśaya), honored by the Lord of Speech, is the supreme goal.
Thus ends the cycle of hyperboles (*atiśayokti*).

When the mode of being of either a sentient or a non-sentient entity, as it actually exists in one way, is imagined in another way, they know that to be *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), as for example: [example follows].
Scorched by the midday sun, the elephant plunges into the lake; I imagine he is intent on uprooting the lotuses that belong to the Sun.
The elephants' plunging into the water to bathe, drink, and eat lotus stalks is described by the poet through poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) as being for the sake of avenging that enmity. (Chapter Two)
"This is an ornament for Karna, who stands in opposition to my future prosperity"—thinking thus, the blue lotus on your ear is likely to wither away at the mere sight of you.
The poet describes the lotus by means of poetic fancy (utprekṣā), wondering whether it is being touched or not by the rays of her glance falling upon the corners of her eyes.
"Darkness seems to smear the limbs; the sky seems to rain collyrium"—this too, for the most part, possesses the characteristics of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).

Yet, due to the presence of the particle *iva*, some people here fall into the error of thinking it is a *upamā* (simile), disregarding the authoritative statement that "there can be no simile with a finite verb (*tiṅanta*)."

The relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison depends upon a common attribute; yet what such an attribute can be perceived here in the case of the verb *limpati* (it smears) and *tamas* (darkness)?

If the act of smearing itself is what is intended, then what else could "he who smears" be? No one who is not insane would claim that the property (dharma) and the possessor of the property (dharmī) are one and the same.
If the agent were to serve as the standard of comparison, he would be subordinated within the verbal action; being occupied with accomplishing his own action, he is unable to look toward another.

Even for one who praises [the darkness] as being equal to the body smeared with oil, saying "his limbs are like that," that common quality [of oiliness] which is not logically connected [to the darkness] must also be sought out.

Just as in the expression "your face is like the moon," beauty is understood [from the word *indu*]; it is not so that something other than the act of smearing is understood here from the root *lip* (to smear).
Let it be observed that, for the purpose of effecting contact with that [darkness], the act of smearing—having the face as its agent and the limbs as its object—is thus imagined by the man.

Poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is manifested by words such as *manye* (I think), *śaṅke* (I suspect), *dhruvam* (certainly), *prāyaḥ* (mostly), *nūnam* (surely), and so forth; the word *iva* (as if) is also of that same nature.

The *hetu* (cause), the *sūkṣma* (the subtle), and the *leśa* (the slight) are the supreme ornaments of speech; the *kāraka* (the producer) and the *śāpaka* (the indicator) are the two types of *hetu*, each of which is manifold in its varieties.
This Malaya breeze, swaying the sprouts of the full-grown sandalwood trees, generates delight in everyone.
In this context, there is an augmentation of that form which is capable of generating affection.
That which is designated as an ornament remains the same even when it has ceased [to function as such].
Having shaken the sandalwood forest and touched the mountain cascades of Malaya, this breeze has arrived to bring relief to travelers. (From the *Kāvyādarśa*)
For such a wind as this is indeed sufficient to bring about non-existence in a person who has developed a distaste for beautiful things due to the fever of separation.

With respect to that [object], causality exists in relation to what is to be extinguished (*nirvartya*) and what is to be modified (*vikārya*); however, in the case of an object to be reached (*prāpya*), causality generally depends solely upon the action (*kriyā*).
The cause for that which is to be accomplished has been shown; now, having provided a pair of examples for the remaining two, the indicative [cause] will be described.
Forests with burgeoning sprouts, ponds with blossoming lotuses, and the full moon—all have been turned into poison for the eyes of the traveler by the God of Love.

Thinking, "I shall make her worthy of honor," the young girl, her eyes askance with a frown of her brows and her lower lip quivering, gazes at her friend who has been placed in the position of a lover.
"The darkness has departed, the moon shines, and the birds go to their roosts"—even this is quite appropriate for announcing the state of the time.
O friend, your mind is clearly understood to be afflicted by love by the heat of your body, which cannot be suppressed by the rays of the moon nor cured by sandalwood water.
Thus have been characterized in their applications the charming indicative causes (*jñāpaka-hetu*). Now, certain captivating non-existence causes (*abhāva-hetu*) are being explained.
Through the lack of practice in the sciences, through lack of association with the wise, and through the failure to restrain the senses, calamity arises for men.
The intoxication of talk about desire has passed; the fever of youth has melted away; delusion is destroyed, O Kṛṣṇā; my mind is fixed upon the holy hermitage.
These are forests, not houses; these are rivers, not women; these are deer, not kinsmen; therefore my mind rejoices.
The conduct of the noble ones is never observed to be utterly non-existent; therefore, all their prosperities increase constantly.
The mango blossoms in the gardens have not yet burst into flower; let a handful of water mixed with sesame seeds be offered to the wives of travelers.

In this context, a real entity—whether in the form of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or other types of absence—functions as the cause for the production of an effect that consists of both existence and non-existence.

The remote cause, the innate cause, the cause immediately following the effect, the cause consisting of what is improper, and the cause consisting of what is proper—thus, the various causes are innumerable.
In these paths of application, there are those which rely on figurative function (*gauṇavṛtti*). This is the second chapter. Extremely beautiful examples of them have been observed, as follows:
O lovely lady, when that victorious weapon of the Bodiless One, known as your sidelong glance, was discharged elsewhere, I am the one who has been wounded in my heart by it.
The age of women, in which childhood has passed away, manifests itself simultaneously with the various delusions and agitations born of love in men.
After the moon’s orb has risen and scattered its rays, the ocean of passion in fawn-eyed women has already surged long before.
O Lord, why does the early morning sunlight of the red glow from Your pair of feet cause the lotus-hands of the Rākṣasas to close like buds?
The rays of the moon-like nails of your feet, pure as jasmine, are able to cause the lotus-hands of kings to close.
